<div class="refresher-question" data-question="1">

### Question 1 · Keep the direction of a difference

Predict the sign and value of `difference`. Which lines assign objects, and which line calculates two means?

```{r refresh-difference, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
control <- c(0.50, 0.60, 0.70)
drought <- c(0.30, 0.40, 0.50)
difference <- mean(drought) - mean(control)
difference
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: calculation and direction</summary>

The difference is `-0.20`: the invented drought mean is `0.40`, the control mean is `0.60`. The first three lines assign objects with `<-`. `mean()` is the function used twice in the third line. The direction is **drought minus control**, so a negative result means a lower drought mean. For a proportion, `-0.20` is a reduction of 20 percentage points.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="2">

### Question 2 · Select rows, keep columns

Read this command in words. What does the blank position after the comma mean?

```{r refresh-rows, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
drought_data <- soil_data[soil_data$remark == "D", ]
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: row selection</summary>

Select rows with `remark` equal to `"D"`, keep all columns, and store them as `drought_data`. Data-frame indexing follows `[rows, columns]`; the empty second position keeps every column. `==` compares values. In yesterday's dataset, this selects drought alone rather than mixtures containing drought.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="3">

### Question 3 · Keep two named columns

What will `selected` contain? Which part combines the column names? What does `dim(selected)` report?

```{r refresh-columns, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
selected <- soil_data[, c("WSA", "PH")]
dim(selected)
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: column selection</summary>

Keep every row and only the columns named `WSA` and `PH`. `c()` combines their names into a character vector. `dim()` reports rows, then columns: for yesterday's full CSV, `353` and `2`. Today we will select four trait columns in the same way.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="4">

### Question 4 · Count missing values

Predict both results. Does `na.rm = TRUE` replace the missing value?

```{r refresh-missing, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
x <- c(2, NA, 4)
sum(is.na(x))
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: missing does not mean zero</summary>

There is `1` missing value. The mean of the two observed values is `3`. `is.na()` identifies missing entries; `sum()` counts the `TRUE` entries. `na.rm = TRUE` excludes the missing value from this calculation; it does not supply a replacement measurement.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="5">

### Question 5 · Extract a result from an object

What do these commands extract? Is the p-value the probability that the null hypothesis is true?

```{r refresh-result, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
test_result$conf.int
test_result$p.value
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: named parts of an analysis result</summary>

`$conf.int` extracts the confidence interval and `$p.value` extracts the p-value. `$` can access named parts of an analysis result as well as columns of a data frame. A p-value describes how unusual a test statistic at least as extreme would be under the null model and its assumptions; it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Today, `$x` and `$rotation` will extract two different parts of a PCA result.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="6">

### Question 6 · A script that runs tomorrow

You saved a plot object named `wsa_plot`, closed RStudio, and reopened an empty session. Why might `ggsave()` now fail? What should your script do before this line?

```{r refresh-script, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
ggsave("WSA_plot.png", plot = wsa_plot)
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: rebuild objects in order</summary>

The new session may have neither `ggplot2` loaded nor `wsa_plot` created. A reproducible script loads the package, imports and prepares the data, creates the plot object, and then saves it. Saving an R script records these steps; saving only a picture does not record the analysis. Run from the beginning to check the order.

</details>
</div>

## 1. Ask about fungal similarity {#question}

**Together · 15 minutes, including the demonstration.** Our ecological question is:

> **Which fungal isolates have similar combinations of traits, and which traits describe the main differences among them?**

A fungal isolate is a particular culture obtained from a fungus. Today each row represents one isolate-level trait record. Different trait measurements in that row are not additional isolates. Some isolates have related taxonomic labels; we will keep their unique IDs rather than treating every row as a different species.

We will examine four traits representing growth, pigmentation, enzyme production and reproduction. Before seeing the results, write a prediction as a comment in your script. For example: “I expect extension and enzyme activity to be associated because ...” Either direction is acceptable if you explain your ecological reasoning. A pattern in these data will not establish its mechanism.

### A small invented example

The instructor will show ten **imaginary** isolates in `Fungal_traits_demo.csv`. This deliberately simple example helps us recognise a pattern. Its values and units are invented; it is not evidence about real fungi and will not be combined with the real dataset.

```{r demo-read, echo=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
demo <- read.csv("Fungal_traits_demo.csv")
demo_names <- c("extension", "melanin", "enz_cel", "spore_abund")
```

```{r demo-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis', purl=FALSE}
knitr::kable(demo, col.names = c("Imaginary isolate", "Extension", "Melanisation", "Enzyme activity", "Spore abundance"))
```

**Discuss before analysis:** choose two similar isolates using at least two traits. Do all four traits use similar numerical ranges? What might happen if we calculate distances directly from these numbers?

<details class="answer"><summary>Discuss: why the numerical scale matters</summary>

For example, Demo_A and Demo_D both have relatively high extension and spore abundance, and low melanisation and enzyme activity in this invented table. Spore abundance has much larger numerical values than the other columns. Without scaling, its numerical differences can dominate Euclidean distances and the first PCA axis. Changing spores to “thousands of spores” would change that influence, despite representing the same biology.

</details>

<details class="plan"><summary>Instructor demonstration: a two-dimensional view</summary>

The left-hand plot shows only two original traits. The PCA plot on the right uses **all four standardised traits** to find new axes. Nearby points have similar displayed coordinates; a two-dimensional view may hide differences in later components. PCA does not require us to assign groups beforehand.

```{r demo-pca, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt='Two plots of ten imaginary isolates: extension versus spores, and PC1 versus PC2 after scaling all four traits.', purl=FALSE}
demo_pca <- prcomp(demo[, demo_names], center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
demo_pct <- 100 * demo_pca$sdev^2 / sum(demo_pca$sdev^2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.3, 2, 1))
plot(demo$extension, demo$spore_abund, pch = 19, col = "#245e49",
     xlab = "Extension (invented scale)", ylab = "Spore abundance (invented scale)",
     main = "Two original traits", ylim = c(0, 1350))
text(demo$extension, demo$spore_abund, labels = sub("Demo_", "", demo$isolate),
     pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
plot(demo_pca$x[, 1], demo_pca$x[, 2], pch = 19, col = "#245e49", asp = 1,
     xlab = paste0("PC1 (", round(demo_pct[1], 1), "%)"),
     ylab = paste0("PC2 (", round(demo_pct[2], 1), "%)"), main = "Four traits summarised")
text(demo_pca$x[, 1], demo_pca$x[, 2], labels = sub("Demo_", "", demo$isolate),
     pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Here PC1 and PC2 display about **97.4%** of the standardised trait variation. The data were constructed to make the pattern easy to see. Real data do not have to form such a neat map.

The instructor can run this compact recipe; students do not need to reproduce this second analysis:

```{r demo-recipe, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
demo <- read.csv("Fungal_traits_demo.csv")
demo_traits <- demo[, c("extension", "melanin", "enz_cel", "spore_abund")]
demo_pca <- prcomp(demo_traits, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
plot(demo_pca$x[, 1], demo_pca$x[, 2], asp = 1,
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", pch = 19)
```

</details>

## 2. Meet the real fungi {#data}

**Purpose:** know what the observations and selected traits represent before analysis.

Unzip the student files, open `ABV_Day3.Rproj`, then open `Day3_starter.R`. Save your script as `Day3_yourname.R` in that folder. The CSV files should sit beside the project file. Load the `ggplot2` package installed earlier in the course. If it is missing, run `install.packages("ggplot2")` once in the Console.

Our teaching file is a column subset of the supplied fungal trait collection. It keeps **all 31 isolate records**, four metadata columns, and the four traits below. We selected traits to cover several biological processes while keeping the first analysis readable. This is a teaching analysis, not a reproduction of the full research paper.

| Column | Biological meaning | How to read the supplied values |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `extension` | Mycelial extension | Higher = greater extension on the processed course scale. |
| `melanin` | Melanisation | Higher = greater melanisation on the supplied course scale. |
| `enz_cel` | Cellobiohydrolase activity | Higher = greater measured activity on the supplied course scale. |
| `spore_abund` | Spore abundance | Higher = greater abundance on the processed course scale. |

**Read this before interpreting units:** the supplied CSV contains processed values and does not document their full transformation history or original raw units. Negative `extension` and `spore_abund` entries are **not negative physical growth or negative spore counts**. Describe relative values on the supplied scales. Do not attach raw units, apply another log transformation, or calculate biological fold changes from these numbers. Consult the original measurement and preprocessing records for such questions. The [downloadable dictionary](Day3_trait_dictionary.csv) records these distinctions; the [study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47705-7) explains the biological traits.

```{r import-real}
library(ggplot2)
file.exists("Fungal_traits_day3.csv")
fungi <- read.csv("Fungal_traits_day3.csv")

dim(fungi)
head(fungi)
trait_names <- c("extension", "melanin", "enz_cel", "spore_abund")
trait_data <- fungi[, trait_names]
str(trait_data)
summary(trait_data)
```

**Do:** identify the isolate ID, metadata, and four analysis columns. Explain why neither `strainID` nor a numeric-looking row number should be treated as a fungal trait.

### Handle missing selected traits transparently

`prcomp()` needs a complete numeric matrix for this workflow. We will retain rows with observations for **all four selected traits**, without replacing missing measurements. A missing value in an unrelated column of the full dataset should not automatically remove an isolate from our four-trait analysis.

```{r missing-traits}
colSums(is.na(trait_data))

keep <- complete.cases(trait_data)
excluded_ids <- fungi$strainID[!keep]
excluded_ids
sum(keep)

fungi_complete <- fungi[keep, ]
trait_matrix <- fungi_complete[, trait_names]
rownames(trait_matrix) <- fungi_complete$strainID
dim(trait_matrix)
```

**New commands:** `colSums()` counts missing entries column by column; `complete.cases()` returns `TRUE` for rows complete across the selected traits. `!keep` reverses that logical selection. We keep metadata and measurements aligned using the **same** `keep` vector.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: dimensions, exclusions and observation unit</summary>

The teaching file has **31 rows and 8 columns**. Each of the four traits has **3 missing values**, occurring in the same three isolates: **DF25, DISC and M**. The analysis retains **28 isolates × 4 traits**. There are four traits per isolate, not 112 independent fungal isolates.

Complete-case exclusion is a transparent choice for this exercise, not a general solution to missing data. The retained isolates may differ systematically from those excluded. We should report the exclusions and avoid assuming that missingness is random.

</details>

<details class="plan"><summary>Optional inspection: look at each trait's distribution</summary>

Use the supplied base-R recipe to inspect the four columns. No normality test is needed before this descriptive PCA. Look for unusual observations and check the data source if something seems inconsistent. Scaling will not remove outliers or correct measurement problems.

```{r inspect-distributions, fig.show='asis', fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5, fig.alt='Four histograms of the selected real fungal traits on their supplied course scales.', purl=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(trait_matrix$extension, main = "Extension", xlab = "Supplied course scale", col = "#dce6d1")
hist(trait_matrix$melanin, main = "Melanisation", xlab = "Supplied course scale", col = "#dce6d1")
hist(trait_matrix$enz_cel, main = "Cellobiohydrolase", xlab = "Supplied course scale", col = "#dce6d1")
hist(trait_matrix$spore_abund, main = "Spore abundance", xlab = "Supplied course scale", col = "#dce6d1")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="data"> I selected four numeric traits, reported exclusions, and kept isolate IDs aligned.</label>

## 3. Put traits on a common scale {#scale}

**Purpose:** prevent arbitrary measurement scales from deciding which traits dominate.

We choose to give each of these four traits the same initial variance weight. For every column, `scale()` subtracts its mean and divides by its sample standard deviation:

**Standardised value = (recorded value − column mean) / column SD.**

This makes each column's mean approximately 0 and SD approximately 1. A value of `+1` means one SD above that column's mean **among the retained isolates**; it does not mean one raw measurement unit. Standardising does not make a skewed distribution normal, remove outliers, or establish equal ecological importance.

```{r scale-real}
trait_scaled <- scale(trait_matrix)

round(colMeans(trait_scaled), 6)
apply(trait_scaled, 2, sd)
```

`apply(..., 2, sd)` is a supplied check: apply the SD calculation to each **column**. You do not need to memorise `apply()` today.

**Do:** explain whether a standardised enzyme value of `+1` and a standardised extension value of `+1` represent equal raw measurements. Why do we standardise these traits for this exercise?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: what scaling changes</summary>

They represent the same relative position—one SD above their respective means—but different biological measurements. The four means should round to 0 and the SDs should be approximately 1. Tiny values such as `1e-16` are numerical rounding near zero.

Scaling is a deliberate analysis choice. When raw variance differences carry the scientific meaning of interest, another choice may be justified. Here, the different supplied scales would otherwise influence both PCA and Euclidean distances arbitrarily.

</details>

<details class="plan"><summary>Optional five-minute check: change a unit, keep the biology</summary>

This uses only the invented dataset. Multiplying its spore values by 1,000 changes the unscaled PCA but leaves the explained variance of a standardised PCA unchanged, apart from numerical rounding. The code is provided as a demonstration; interpreting the outcome is the task.

```{r demo-units, purl=FALSE}
demo <- read.csv("Fungal_traits_demo.csv")
demo_traits <- demo[, trait_names]
demo_other_units <- demo_traits
demo_other_units$spore_abund <- demo_other_units$spore_abund * 1000

summary(prcomp(demo_traits, scale. = FALSE))
summary(prcomp(demo_other_units, scale. = FALSE))
summary(prcomp(demo_traits, scale. = TRUE))
summary(prcomp(demo_other_units, scale. = TRUE))
```

**Discuss:** why would an analysis that changes because we express the same measurement in different units be difficult to interpret ecologically?

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="scale"> I can explain a standardised value and our reason for scaling.</label>

## 4. Build a PCA map of the isolates {#pca}

**Purpose:** summarise several correlated traits with a few new axes, without assigning groups in advance.

**Principal component analysis (PCA)** finds new axes that summarise variation. PC1 captures the greatest possible variation along one axis. PC2 captures the greatest remaining variation while being perpendicular to PC1. With these four traits, there can be up to four nonzero components. We will display the first two and check how much information they retain.

```{r run-pca}
pca_result <- prcomp(trait_scaled, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
summary(pca_result)

variance_percent <- 100 * pca_result$sdev^2 / sum(pca_result$sdev^2)
variance_table <- data.frame(
  PC = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "PC4"),
  percent = variance_percent
)
variance_table
sum(variance_percent[1:2])
```

We already centred and scaled `trait_scaled`, so `center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE` avoids doing that preparation again. `$sdev^2` gives the component variances; dividing by their sum gives their shares. This calculation is a supplied recipe rather than a formula you must reproduce from memory.

### Scores are coordinates of isolates

`pca_result$x` contains the **scores**: each isolate's position on the new axes. We attach the matching IDs from the retained rows. The order has not changed.

```{r pca-scores}
scores <- data.frame(
  strainID = fungi_complete$strainID,
  PC1 = pca_result$x[, 1],
  PC2 = pca_result$x[, 2]
)
head(scores)
```

Use the supplied plotting recipe. We label four example isolates to keep the figure readable; every retained isolate is still shown. `coord_equal()` gives the same length to one unit on either axis.

```{r pca-plot}
label_data <- scores[scores$strainID %in% c("A", "DF56", "C31", "DF36"), ]

pca_plot <- ggplot(scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#245e49", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(data = label_data, aes(label = strainID), vjust = -0.8, size = 3.5) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(variance_percent[1], 1), "% of variance)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(variance_percent[2], 1), "% of variance)"),
    title = "Similarities among 28 fungal isolates",
    subtitle = "PCA of four standardised traits; four example IDs labelled"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
pca_plot
```

**Do before opening the check:** record the PC1 and PC2 percentages and their sum. Find isolates A and DF56. Are they close together in this displayed map? Does the plot show all trait variation?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: explained variation and reference figure</summary>

For this four-trait selection, **PC1 explains about 55.0%**, **PC2 about 19.1%**, and together they show **74.1%** of the standardised trait variation. The remaining **25.9%** lies in PC3 and PC4. This is variation in the selected traits among retained isolates—not the percentage of soil functioning or fungal ecology that we have explained.

```{r reference-pca, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.5, fig.alt='PCA of 28 real fungal isolates. PC1 explains 55.0 percent and PC2 19.1 percent of selected-trait variance. Isolate A and DF56 lie far apart on PC1.', purl=FALSE}
print(pca_plot)
```

A and DF56 are far apart along PC1. Two points close in PC1–PC2 can still differ in later components. A PCA plot describes patterns; it does not test a treatment effect or establish distinct biological groups.

Your axes may be reflected compared with the reference. A PC's sign is arbitrary: reversing both its scores and loadings leaves the relationships unchanged. Compare relative positions and trait associations, rather than memorising “left” or “right.”

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="pca"> I made a PCA map and can state the variation displayed and omitted.</label>

## 5. Connect the axes back to traits {#interpret}

**Purpose:** turn a pattern on a graph into an evidence-based ecological description.

The PCA result contains two different things:

| Part of the result | R command | What it describes |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Scores** | `pca_result$x` | Coordinates of **isolates** on the PC axes. |
| **Loadings** | `pca_result$rotation` | Weights of **traits** in those axes. |

Extract only the two loading columns needed for the figure:

```{r pca-loadings}
loadings <- pca_result$rotation[, 1:2]
round(loadings, 2)
```

For one component, larger **absolute** weights indicate greater involvement in that axis. Traits with the same sign point in the same direction along that component; opposite signs represent a contrast. Read a loading **together with the isolate's score**, then check the recorded trait values. These weights are not p-values or percentages, and they are not automatically correlations with the PCs.

### Your task: compare two isolates

1. Describe the PC1 contrast using the signs of all four loadings.
2. Predict which of A and DF56 has greater extension and spore abundance on the supplied scales.
3. Check the prediction using the original records below.
4. Use two trait values to support your description. Identify one conclusion the PCA cannot establish.

```{r compare-isolates}
fungi_complete[fungi_complete$strainID %in% c("A", "DF56"),
               c("strainID", trait_names)]
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: a possible trait interpretation</summary>

With the reference signs, PC1 gives positive weights to **extension (+0.50)** and **spore abundance (+0.53)** and negative weights to **melanisation (−0.49)** and **cellobiohydrolase activity (−0.48)**. PC1 therefore summarises a contrast between these combinations. All four traits contribute appreciably; avoid treating it as a measurement of one trait alone.

DF56 has higher extension and spore values than A on the supplied processed scales. For example, extension is approximately **2.373 versus −0.862**, while melanisation is approximately **0.210 versus 0.449**. A has higher cellobiohydrolase activity (**2.312 versus 0.963**). These observations support a relative trait description; they do not quantify a raw-unit growth difference or establish that one isolate performs better in soil.

PC2 mainly contrasts melanisation and cellobiohydrolase activity, which have opposite signs on this component. A reflected PC gives the same ecological contrast with its signs reversed.

It is reasonable to propose a hypothesis about different resource-use strategies. These observations alone do not establish a physiological trade-off, causal mechanism, adaptation to drought, or performance under field conditions.

</details>

<details class="plan"><summary>Optional: see trait weights as bars</summary>

The same loading table is shown below. The horizontal axis is a trait weight, not an effect size. You can interpret this figure without reproducing the plotting code.

```{r loading-bars, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4, fig.alt='Separate PC1 and PC2 loading plots for four fungal traits, showing opposite directions of trait weights.', purl=FALSE}
loading_data <- data.frame(
  trait = rep(c("Extension", "Melanisation", "Cellobiohydrolase", "Spore abundance"), 2),
  component = rep(c("PC1", "PC2"), each = 4),
  weight = c(loadings[, 1], loadings[, 2])
)
ggplot(loading_data, aes(x = weight, y = trait)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey65") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = weight, yend = trait), colour = "#6a8f62", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = "#245e49", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~component) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.8, 0.8)) +
  labs(x = "Trait weight (loading)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

</details>

**Discuss together:** if someone calls all isolates on one side “drought-tolerant fungi,” what measurement is missing from our four-trait analysis? What would you need to test that claim?

<details class="answer"><summary>Possible answer: measured traits and untested claims</summary>

We did not include a drought response measurement in this PCA. Growth, pigmentation or enzyme activity may motivate a hypothesis, but they do not themselves demonstrate drought tolerance. We would need a clearly defined drought-response measurement and a suitable replicated experiment or independent validation. Even then, we should distinguish performance in culture from performance in field soil.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="interpret"> I connected isolate positions to at least two traits and stated a limit to the interpretation.</label>

<div class="break-note">Break · Save your script and take 10 minutes. When you return, explain the difference between a score and a loading to a neighbour.</div>

## 6. Explore a clustering tree {#cluster}

**Purpose:** explore how a distance-based method groups similar isolate records.

PCA gives a continuous map. **Hierarchical clustering** begins with each isolate separately, then successively joins isolates or groups according to a rule. The resulting **dendrogram** shows those joins.

We will use Euclidean distance from **all four scaled traits**, followed by **complete linkage**. For complete linkage, the distance between two groups is the largest pairwise distance across their members. These are stated analysis choices, not automatic biological truths.

```{r cluster-tree}
trait_distances <- dist(trait_scaled, method = "euclidean")
cluster_tree <- hclust(trait_distances, method = "complete")

plot(cluster_tree, labels = fungi_complete$strainID,
     main = "Fungal similarity in four standardised traits",
     xlab = "Isolate ID", sub = "Euclidean distance; complete linkage",
     ylab = "Complete-linkage distance", cex = 0.75)
```

Read the **height of a join** using the stated distance rule; the left-to-right order of labels is not a separate ecological gradient. This is a tree of selected-trait similarity, **not a phylogenetic tree**.

### Compare two exploratory cuts

```{r cut-tree}
groups_k2 <- cutree(cluster_tree, k = 2)
groups_k3 <- cutree(cluster_tree, k = 3)

membership <- data.frame(
  strainID = fungi_complete$strainID,
  k2 = groups_k2,
  k3 = groups_k3
)
membership
table(groups_k3)
table(k2 = groups_k2, k3 = groups_k3)
```

**Do:** identify a group at `k = 2` that splits at `k = 3`. Record its isolate IDs. Does asking for three clusters demonstrate that three natural fungal strategies exist? Would the result necessarily stay the same if we changed traits or linkage method?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: tree, memberships and interpretation</summary>

```{r reference-tree, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=8, fig.height=4.8, fig.alt='Complete-linkage dendrogram for 28 fungal isolates, with three exploratory groups outlined.', purl=FALSE}
plot(cluster_tree, labels = fungi_complete$strainID,
     main = "One possible cut: k = 3", xlab = "Isolate ID",
     sub = "Groups depend on the selected traits, scaling and clustering rule",
     ylab = "Complete-linkage distance", cex = 0.75)
rect.hclust(cluster_tree, k = 3, border = "#6a8f62")
```

The three groups have **5, 17 and 6 isolates** with the reference numbering. The 11-member group at `k = 2` splits into groups of 5 and 6 at `k = 3`. The other 17-member group stays together. Match IDs and memberships; cluster numbers themselves have no ranking or biological meaning.

The algorithm gives us the requested number of groups. This does **not** prove that three discrete ecological strategies exist. Trait selection, scaling, unusual observations and the linkage rule can affect the result. Continuous biological variation can also be divided into clusters.

</details>

### Place these memberships on the PCA map

The grouping was calculated from all four traits. We can now colour the two-dimensional PCA map by that membership; we do not recalculate clusters from PC1 and PC2 alone.

```{r colour-clusters}
scores$cluster <- factor(groups_k3)

cluster_plot <- ggplot(scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = cluster, shape = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.9) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#245e49", "#b67931", "#6266a4")) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(variance_percent[1], 1), "% of variance)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(variance_percent[2], 1), "% of variance)"),
    title = "An exploratory grouping on the PCA map",
    subtitle = "Memberships calculated from all four scaled traits",
    colour = "Cluster (k = 3)", shape = "Cluster (k = 3)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
cluster_plot
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: the coloured map is another view of the same data</summary>

```{r reference-clusters, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.3, fig.alt='PCA map coloured and shaped by the three exploratory clusters calculated from all four scaled traits.', purl=FALSE}
print(cluster_plot)
```

Apparent separation here is **not independent validation**: the PCA and clusters use the same underlying traits. The two-dimensional projection may also hide differences that contributed to clustering. We have not performed a significance test of group separation.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="cluster"> I compared two cuts and can explain what the dendrogram and group labels represent.</label>

## 7. Your turn: describe one group using evidence {#apply}

**Independent task · 10 minutes.** Choose one of the three groups. Describe its trait profile, rather than assigning it a strategy name based on its colour or number.

Use this supplied recipe to calculate average **standardised trait values** for each group. `aggregate()` applies the mean separately within each group; these are descriptive summaries, not tests.

```{r cluster-profiles}
cluster_profiles <- aggregate(
  as.data.frame(trait_scaled),
  by = list(cluster = factor(groups_k3)),
  FUN = mean
)
cluster_profiles
```

Write answers in your script:

1. How many isolates belong to your chosen group? Name two of them.
2. Which two traits best support your description? Quote their group means on the standardised scale.
3. Check those traits in the recorded values for the group's individual isolates. Are all members identical? How would you describe within-group variation?
4. What further observation or experiment would help test an ecological hypothesis suggested by this profile?

Adapt the two blanks below. Do the task before opening the example answer. This template is not meant to run until you replace both `???` placeholders.

```{r own-group-template, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
chosen_group <- ???
fungi_complete[groups_k3 == chosen_group,
               c("strainID", "extension", "melanin", "enz_cel", "spore_abund")]

# My description, supported by two trait values: ???
```

<details class="answer"><summary>One possible answer: the five-isolate group</summary>

The group containing **A, C21, C29, DF35 and DF36** has higher average melanisation (**about +1.80 SD**), lower extension (**−1.08 SD**) and lower spore abundance (**−1.22 SD**) than the overall retained sample. These are group means on the standardised course scales. Members still vary in their individual traits; the grouping does not make every member identical.

To inspect these five records directly:

```{r group-example, purl=FALSE}
fungi_complete[fungi_complete$strainID %in% c("A", "C21", "C29", "DF35", "DF36"),
               c("strainID", trait_names)]
```

A possible hypothesis is that their pigmentation and growth profile relates to performance under a particular environmental stress. Test that with a defined stress treatment, a matched control and replication; the present grouping alone does not demonstrate stress tolerance. Other group descriptions are equally acceptable when supported by their trait values.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="apply"> I wrote my own group description using trait values and proposed a follow-up test.</label>

## 8. Save a reproducible analysis and explain it {#save}

**Purpose:** leave a record that another student can check and you can rerun.

The script below saves figures and tables in an `outputs` folder. The score table includes IDs and all four PC coordinates so the record retains more than the displayed two-dimensional map. Cluster labels remain descriptive labels.

```{r save-results}
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)

scores_export <- data.frame(
  strainID = fungi_complete$strainID,
  pca_result$x,
  cluster_k2 = groups_k2,
  cluster_k3 = groups_k3
)
loadings_export <- data.frame(trait = rownames(loadings), loadings)

write.csv(scores_export, "outputs/Day3_PCA_scores_and_clusters.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(loadings_export, "outputs/Day3_PC1_PC2_loadings.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(variance_table, "outputs/Day3_variance_explained.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(cluster_profiles, "outputs/Day3_cluster_profiles_scaled.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(fungi_complete, "outputs/Day3_retained_trait_records.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(strainID = excluded_ids), "outputs/Day3_excluded_isolates.csv", row.names = FALSE)

ggsave("outputs/Day3_PCA.png", plot = pca_plot, width = 7.5, height = 5.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
ggsave("outputs/Day3_PCA_clusters.png", plot = cluster_plot, width = 7.5, height = 5.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

png("outputs/Day3_dendrogram.png", width = 2400, height = 1500, res = 300)
plot(cluster_tree, labels = fungi_complete$strainID,
     main = "Fungal similarity in four standardised traits",
     xlab = "Isolate ID", sub = "Euclidean distance; complete linkage; k = 3",
     ylab = "Complete-linkage distance", cex = 0.75)
rect.hclust(cluster_tree, k = 3, border = "#6a8f62")
dev.off()
```

### Write four or five sentences

Use your own words. Include:

- the ecological question, four traits and number of retained isolates;
- the reason for standardising and the percentage shown by PC1–PC2;
- one isolate or group comparison supported by at least two traits;
- the exploratory nature of the grouping and one limitation or follow-up question.

<details class="answer"><summary>A possible report structure</summary>

“We explored similarities among 28 fungal isolates using extension, melanisation, cellobiohydrolase activity and spore abundance. We standardised the supplied trait values to give each trait equal initial variance weight, and the first two PCA axes displayed 74.1% of this variation. [Insert your comparison and two supporting trait values here.] Complete-linkage clustering offered one way to summarise similarities, but choosing three groups does not establish three natural strategies. [Insert a limitation or an experiment that would test your ecological interpretation.]”

Possible limitations include the four-trait selection, omitted isolates, variation outside PC1–PC2, processed measurement scales, or the need to validate culture-based trait patterns in field conditions. Avoid copying a strategy label without evidence.

</details>

### Final check: restart and explain

Save your script, choose **Session → Restart R** in RStudio, and run the required analysis from its first line. It should import the data, recreate the figures and write the outputs without relying on objects left in your Environment.

Answer these exit questions without looking back:

1. What is the difference between an isolate's **score** and a trait's **loading**?
2. Why might two nearby points in the plot differ in the original four traits?
3. Does a cluster number tell us how well a fungus performs in soil?
4. Which measurement or experiment would you add next, and why?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check your main ideas</summary>

A score locates an isolate on a PC axis; a loading weights a trait in that axis. A two-dimensional projection leaves variation in later PCs. Cluster numbers are arbitrary identifiers for one grouping, not performance rankings or proof of natural strategies. A useful next measurement follows from a stated ecological hypothesis and a design that can test it.

</details>

## Optional: how does the question change when traits change? {#extra}

**Only after the required work.** A PCA represents the traits we choose to include. Explore a different, explicitly stated question by adding the supplied `hyphal_diam` trait. This activity is about sensitivity to trait choice; adding a trait does not automatically improve an analysis.

Download [the original full course file](Fungal_traits_full.csv) into your project folder. The names below select the original four traits plus hyphal diameter. To isolate the effect of adding a trait, we keep the **same 28 isolate IDs** and check that the new matrix is complete. This avoids silently changing both traits and observations.

```{r optional-fifth-trait, purl=FALSE}
full_fungi <- read.csv("Fungal_traits_full.csv")
same_isolates <- full_fungi[match(fungi_complete$strainID, full_fungi$strainID), ]
five_names <- c(trait_names, "hyphal_diam")
five_traits <- same_isolates[, five_names]
stopifnot(identical(same_isolates$strainID, fungi_complete$strainID))
stopifnot(all(complete.cases(five_traits)))

five_pca <- prcomp(five_traits, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
summary(five_pca)
round(five_pca$rotation[, 1:2], 2)
```

**Discuss:** how did the explained variation and trait weights change? Are you still answering exactly the same question? Would retaining two components necessarily preserve the same fraction of information after adding a trait?

Do not begin by selecting every numeric column of the full dataset. An index column is not a trait, and derived indices such as `decompPC1` or `stress_tolPC1` already summarise other measurements. Including a summary alongside all its components changes how that biological domain is weighted. The full dataset needs a separate plan, data dictionary and preprocessing review.

<details class="plan"><summary>Optional: combine points and trait arrows in a biplot</summary>

After understanding scores and loadings separately, you can view them together:

```{r optional-biplot, fig.show='asis', fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.5, fig.alt='Optional biplot combining isolate positions and four trait arrows. Observation and variable coordinates use different scales.', purl=FALSE}
biplot(pca_result, choices = c(1, 2), scale = 0,
       xlabs = fungi_complete$strainID, cex = c(0.6, 0.9),
       main = "Optional biplot: isolate scores and trait directions")
```

The arrows show trait directions under the chosen biplot scaling. Observation coordinates and arrow coordinates use different scales; do not read a point-to-arrow distance as a biological distance, interpret arrow length as ecological importance, or assume an arrow angle gives an exact correlation when only two PCs are displayed. The loading table and original trait values remain useful checks.

</details>

## Help, downloads and references {#help}

<details class="plan"><summary>Something did not run?</summary>

- **File not found:** open `ABV_Day3.Rproj` from the extracted folder. Check `getwd()`, `list.files()` and `file.exists("Fungal_traits_day3.csv")`. The ZIP must be extracted first.
- **Object not found:** run the required earlier chunks in order. R distinguishes uppercase and lowercase names. The optional demonstration uses separate `demo` objects and is not needed for the real-data analysis.
- **Package missing:** install `ggplot2` once, then load it in each fresh session. Neither `plotly` nor `ggfortify` is required.
- **Missing values in PCA:** check `complete.cases()` on the four selected traits and use `trait_matrix` or `trait_scaled`, not the original incomplete data frame.
- **Cannot rescale a constant column:** inspect the selected columns. Standardisation requires nonzero variation; investigate the column and its meaning before deciding whether to exclude it.
- **Labels do not match points:** apply the same row selection to metadata and trait values. Do not sort one without the other.
- **My PCA faces the other way:** check whether scores and corresponding loadings are both reflected. Axis signs alone are arbitrary.
- **Cluster labels seem different:** compare isolate memberships and profiles, not the numbers assigned to groups.

</details>

**Data and research context:** the real teaching file retains selected columns and all rows from the course's `Fungal_traits.csv`, supplied by Mohan Bi; no values were imputed. See Camenzind et al. (2024), [*Towards establishing a fungal economics spectrum in soil saprobic fungi*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47705-7), for the trait framework and original study methods. The small demonstration dataset is deliberately invented for this lesson.

**R references:** [PCA with `prcomp()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/prcomp.html), [standardising with `scale()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/scale.html), [hierarchical clustering](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/hclust.html), and [cutting a tree](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/cutree.html).
